chapter_theme: Neythal: on the sea shore the heroine grieves the shore lord's absence and the doubtful worth of his secret oath and signs (41-45, 49, 50), the friend presses him to marry by appeal to what is fitting and to his name (46, 48), and the hero is struck by the fisher girl guarding the drying catch (47).

41.reading: Since the lord of the clear sea's shore has gone away, the heroine tells her bright-jewelled friend that her wide bright eyes, sunk in grief, will not sleep: the flower-crested anril cries out though its mate has come close and rests beside it, so what wonder if she, whose mate is gone, keeps awake?
41.nuance: The optative துஞ்சற்க can be read as the heroine's vow of wakefulness or as the friend's gentle irony; either way the argument runs from the lesser case to the greater: a bird that cries with its mate beside it licenses a parted woman's sleepless crying.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea-shore lord and the anril of the palmyra shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from ஒள்ளிழாய் and the grief of line 1

iraicchi.act: the anril cries out in the night even while its mate rests close beside it
iraicchi.sense: if a joined bird laments, the heroine parted from her man cannot be asked to sleep

42.reading: The heroine begs the crooked-legged crab, as a favour, not to walk over and blur the tracks the long chariot of the lord of the ever-roaring shore left behind, so that she may look at the path he took until her eyes are full.
42.nuance: All she has left of him is the wheel-rut in the sand, and the only creature that can take it from her is the crab, so she pleads with it as with a person (குறையாம் இரப்பேம்).

thinai_evidence.note: the roaring sea's shore and its crab

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the crab on the shore; the colophon gives no thurai

43.reading: Climbing the long striped sand where the punnai has put out buds like the eggs of a speckled lizard, the heroine says that if the cool lord of the low-lying sea is to grant her his garlanded chest, she and her friend will surely see it in the circle drawn in the sand.
43.nuance: ஆழி is taken as the circle a waiting woman draws in the sand to divine whether the lover will come; it can also mean the sea, which would change the last line to seeing him by the sea, so the reading is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai on the dunes and the sea-shore lord

comparisons.tenor: the punnai's buds, as if the tree had laid a speckled lizard's eggs

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the hoped-for gift of his chest points to marriage still to come

44.reading: The heroine tells her friend that she wept till her kohl-lined eyes reddened, gazing at the cool flowering grove the shore lord had left, and when her mother saw her face and asked what grieved her, she answered that the sea had come and wrecked her sand-house.
44.nuance: The lie is also the truth in code: it was the man of the sea, the கொண்கன், who came and broke up her girlhood play, so the excuse names the real cause in terms only the friend can read.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord and the sea that comes up the sand

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she reports to the friend how she hid the affair from the mother

45.reading: The heroine tells her friend, whose body is tender as a mango shoot, that the cool lord of the dark backwater came to her in the moist grove, took her bangled arm and swore his faith, and asks whether the herons of that flowering grove will really let the oath go by.
45.nuance: The herons are called on as the only witnesses of a secret oath; they are the subject of her question, not a carrier of a further sense, so they are not tagged iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater lord and the herons of the shore grove

comparisons.tenor: the friend's body, tender and coloured like a young mango leaf

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; she recalls the oath given in secret

46.reading: The friend asks the lord of the seaside grove, where innocent young girls light their sand-houses with cool pearls heaped up by the tide of the roaring sea, whether it befits him to make her friend's shoulders lose their beauty.
46.nuance: The girls treat the sea's pearls as playthings, which sets the heroine's guarded girlhood against his careless use of her beauty; read as ullurai it gives only that one pair (precious things spent lightly), so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the tide-washed shore and its grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; she reproaches him for delaying, as one pressing for marriage

47.reading: The hero says that the bright-jewelled girl who scares the birds off the fat fish her brothers brought in together, casting their fine nets till the great sea was stirred to its depths, has become a tormenting goddess to him beyond bearing.
47.nuance: The brothers' nets, cast together, place the girl inside her watchful kin from the first line, which is why the sight of her is fear as much as desire.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishing people's nets and their drying catch

comparisons.tenor: the maiden, who becomes for him an afflicting goddess

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; he speaks of his own state (எமக்கு), perhaps for the friend to hear

48.reading: The friend asks the cool lord of the long backwater, where pearls brought by the tide onto the heaped sand of the dunes stay and glitter, whether men who do not take up the distress of those who have come to depend on them can carry great renown.
48.nuance: The pearl the tide leaves on the dune keeps shining where it was set down; the friend wants the girl who has come to him to be kept so. That is one pair only, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the dunes and the long backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; she presses him to marry by appeal to his name

49.reading: The heroine says that the lord of the clear sea's shore, where the bright flower of the thorny-fronded thaazhai opens among its leaves like a lump of butter and the whole shore round about smells as if a god dwelt there, gave her a sign she cannot trust.
49.nuance: The place of the tryst is so fragrant it seems holy, while the man's signal there is the one thing on that shore that is not clear (தெளி-கடல் against தெளியாக் குறி).

thinai_evidence.note: the thaazhai of the shore grove and the sea-shore lord

comparisons.tenor: the opened white thaazhai flower among its fronds, like butter

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; the sign (குறி) is the tryst signal

50.reading: The heroine tells her bright-jewelled friend that she rose and went out, thinking it the sound of the bells on the horses yoked to the chariot of the cool lord of the lovely sea, and turned back, her heart melting within her, when she heard it was only the noise of fruit-seeking birds.
50.nuance: The birds that crave fruit mirror her own craving: she too goes out at a sound, and both are disappointed waiters.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon thurai; she waits for his coming

links.note: Akananuru 50: the hidden-tearful girl says the anril on the palmyra by the house cannot sleep at night if parted even once from its mate. Ainthinai Aimpathu 41: the anril cries though its mate has come and rests beside it.
links.teaches: The anril's wakefulness is a fixed proof of sleepless separation, and the venba reverses its case: the long poem argues from a parted bird by likeness, the four-line poem from a joined bird by greater reason, so the same bird can carry both the analogy and the a fortiori.

links.note: In Akananuru 170 the woman begs the crab to carry her word to the shore lord, since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 42 she begs the crab not to trample his chariot's tracks.
links.teaches: Taken together they show why the crab is the neythal heroine's confidant: it alone moves where the lover moved, so she can ask it either to carry her word to him or to spare the one trace of him she still has.

links.note: Natrinai 378: the bond began when the shore lord came and broke up their little striped sand-house and spoke soft words. Ainthinai Aimpathu 44: the weeping girl tells her mother that the sea came and wrecked her sand-house.
links.teaches: Natrinai 378 shows that the wrecked sand-house is the very scene where the secret love began, which turns the girl's excuse in Ainthinai Aimpathu 44 into a coded confession: the 'sea' that broke her play is the man of the sea.

links.note: Kuruntokai 25: no one but the thief was there, and only a heron watching for aaral fish, so if he lies she has no recourse. Ainthinai Aimpathu 45: will the herons of the grove let his oath go? On a plain reading one heron is no witness and the other herons are.
links.teaches: The same bird stands at the secret oath in both, but Kuruntokai's heron, intent on its fish, proves that a kalavu vow has no witness, while the venba's herons are made guarantors, so the pair shows the heroine's two answers to the oathless union: despair, or a trust that invents its witnesses.

links.note: Natrinai 283 and Ainthinai Aimpathu 46 both have the friend ask the shore lord, beside girls decking their sand-houses (with neythal flowers, with pearls), whether it is fitting (தகுமோ, தகுவதோ) that the girl's beauty should waste.
links.teaches: The friend's reproach has a fixed form, the girls' sand-house play set against the heroine's wasting beauty with the question 'is it fitting?', and Natrinai adds the ground the venba leaves implicit: his word was held truer than the sun, so the wasting is a breach of his truth.

links.note: In Akananuru 80 the friend tells the shore lord that they spend the day scaring birds from the fish their father brought, and bids him come by day; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 47 the hero sees the girl scaring birds from the fish her brothers brought and finds her a tormenting goddess.
links.teaches: Guarding the drying catch is the neythal girl's appointed work and so the one place she is seen by day: the friend can offer it as a meeting place, while the hero's first sight of her there already places her among the kinsmen whose catch she guards, which is why the sight brings fear.

links.note: Naladiyar 203: the great never say they will not support those who have come to depend on them (தற்சேர்ந் தவரை), as a branch bears its own fruit. Ainthinai Aimpathu 48: can those who do not hold to the distress of those who have come to depend on them (தற்சேர்ந்தார்) carry great renown?
links.teaches: The shared word தற்சேர்ந்தார் shows the friend borrowing the maxim of supporting one's dependents and turning it on the lover: the girl in secret love is made a dependent with a kinsman's claim, and his renown is staked on marrying her.

links.note: In Akananuru 4 the returning man has tied his chariot's bell-tongues so as not to startle the paired birds sleeping in the flowering boughs; in Ainthinai Aimpathu 50 the waiting girl takes the noise of birds for his horses' bells.
links.teaches: Held together, the two poems make the chariot bell the sound by which each lover's attention is measured: the man who has come home to his wife silences it out of care for mated birds, while the girl still in secret love hears it in every bird.
